09.01.title: Atomic bonding and stiffness
09.01.html:
Why is steel about 200 times stiffer than rubber and 3 times stiffer than aluminium? Young’s modulus is not a property you can change by heat treatment or cold work, unlike strength. It’s set by the bonds between atoms: how steeply the energy rises when you pull two atoms apart.

The pair potential

Two atoms attract at long range and repel strongly when their electron clouds overlap. A classic model is the Lennard-Jones potential:

V(r)=4ε[(rσ​)12−(rσ​)6].

It has a minimum of depth ε at r0​=21/6σ, the equilibrium spacing. The force between the atoms is F=−dV/dr, which is zero at r0​.

Stiffness is curvature

Expand V around r0​:

V(r)≈−ε+21​S(r−r0​)2,S=dr2d2V​​r0​​.

So for small stretches each bond is a linear spring of stiffness S: Hooke’s law, straight from the shape of the energy well. For Lennard-Jones, S=72ε/(21/3σ2)=57.1ε/σ2.

From bonds to Young’s modulus

In a simple cubic packing, each bond carries the load on an area of about r02​, and a strain ϵ stretches it by ϵr0​. Stress =Sϵr0​/r02​, so

E≈r0​S​.

Covalent and metallic bonds have S of about 20 to 200 N/m at r0​≈0.25 nm, giving E of 80 to 800 GPa: metals and ceramics. Weak van der Waals bonds, as in solid argon or between polymer chains, have S≈1 N/m and give E of a few GPa. Rubber is softer still because it doesn’t stretch bonds at all, it uncoils chains.

Two bonus results

  • The attraction is largest at 1.109r0​. That maximum force sets a theoretical strength of roughly E/10 to E/30. Real materials fail far below it, for reasons covered in 09.03 and 09.12.
  • The well is steeper on the inside than the outside. A vibrating (hot) pair spends its time further apart on average: thermal expansion.

Worked exampleArgon, from potential to modulus

ε=1.65×10−21 J (10.3 meV), σ=0.340 nm.

  1. r0​=21/6⋅0.340=0.3816 nm.
  2. Bond stiffness: the analytic formula gives 0.8157 N/m, and a central finite difference of V gives 0.8157 N/m. The slope of the force at r0​ is −S, as it should be.
  3. E≈S/r0​=2.14 GPa. Measured values for solid argon are about 1 to 3 GPa.
  4. Peak attraction 11.63 pN at 1.1087r0​ (strain 0.109). Stress estimate 80 MPa, which is E/26.8.
  5. Vibrating with 5 % of the well depth, the turning points are 0.9669 and 1.0431 r0​, so the midpoint moves out to 1.0050 r0​. At 20 %, 1.0220 r0​. That growth is thermal expansion.
  6. A metal-like bond with S=50 N/m at 0.25 nm gives E≈200 GPa, about right for steel.

Exercise 1A stiffer bond

A diamond C–C bond has a stiffness of about 470 N/m at r0​=0.154 nm. Estimate Young’s modulus with E≈S/r0​ and compare it with the measured 1050 to 1200 GPa.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. E≈470/0.154×10−9=3.05×1012 Pa, about 3000 GPa.
  2. That is about 2.7 times the measured value. The simple-cubic picture assumes every bond lines up with the load. In diamond’s tetrahedral network the bonds are tilted, so they also bend and rotate, and fewer bonds cross each square metre. The estimate gets the order of magnitude right, which is what it is for.

quiz.q: Lennard-Jones bond stiffness for ε = 1.65e-21 J, σ = 0.34 nm (N/m). 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 72ε/(21/3σ2).

quiz.q: Equilibrium spacing r₀ (nm) for σ = 0.34 nm. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: r0​=21/6σ.

quiz.q: Young’s modulus estimate (GPa) for S = 50 N/m at r₀ = 0.25 nm.
quiz.explain: E≈S/r0​.

quiz.q: Young’s modulus of a metal is changed significantly by…
quiz.explain: Strength changes; stiffness barely does.
options: Almost none of these: it is set by the bonds

quiz.q: Thermal expansion comes from…
quiz.explain: Hotter atoms spend more time at larger spacing.
options: The asymmetry of the energy well

09.02.title: Crystal structures
09.02.html:
A Swiss watch spring, an aluminium bike frame and a copper wire are all crystals: their atoms sit on a regular three-dimensional grid. Which grid a metal chooses decides a lot. Copper and aluminium (face-centred cubic) are ductile even at low temperature, iron at room temperature (body-centred cubic) can turn brittle in the cold, and titanium and magnesium (hexagonal) are harder to form.

Unit cells

A crystal is a small unit cell repeated in all directions. For metals, model the atoms as hard spheres of radius R that touch their nearest neighbours. Three cubic cells, with lattice constant a:

lattice atoms per cell atoms touch along R coordination
simple cubic (SC) 1 edge a/2 6
body-centred cubic (BCC) 2 body diagonal 3​a/4 8
face-centred cubic (FCC) 4 face diagonal 2​a/4 12

Atoms on corners are shared by 8 cells, those on faces by 2. So FCC has 8⋅81​+6⋅21​=4 atoms per cell.

Packing factor

The atomic packing factor is the fraction of space filled by atoms:

APF=a3n⋅34​πR3​.

For FCC, 4⋅34​π(2​a/4)3/a3=π/18​=0.7405, the densest possible packing of equal spheres. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) stacks the same close-packed layers in a different order and reaches the same 0.7405. BCC gives 0.680, SC only 0.524 (polonium is the only element that uses it).

Density from the lattice

ρ=NA​a3nA​,

with A the molar mass. X-ray diffraction measures a very precisely, so this links atomic structure to bulk density.

Worked exampleBuilding lattices in code

  1. The code generates lattice points, counts neighbours at the smallest distance, and computes the packing factor from the formula and by Monte Carlo (400,000 random points in the cell):
lattice coordination APF formula APF Monte Carlo
SC 6 0.5236 0.5235
BCC 8 0.6802 0.6803
FCC 12 0.7405 0.7403
  1. HCP with the ideal c/a=1.6330: coordination 12 and APF 0.7405, equal to π/18​.
  2. Densities: iron (BCC, a=0.28665 nm) 7.874 g/cm³; copper (FCC, 0.36149 nm) 8.935 g/cm³; aluminium (FCC, 0.40495 nm) 2.699 g/cm³. All match handbook values.

Exercise 1Nickel

Nickel is FCC with an atomic radius of 0.1246 nm and a molar mass of 58.69 g/mol. Find the lattice constant and the density.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4R=2​a, so a=4⋅0.1246/2​=0.3524 nm.
  2. ρ=4⋅58.69/(6.022×1023⋅(0.3524×10−7 cm)3)=8.91 g/cm³ (handbook value 8.90).

quiz.q: Packing factor of FCC. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: π/18​.

quiz.q: Packing factor of BCC. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 2⋅34​π(3​/4)3.

quiz.q: Density (g/cm³) of nickel from a = 0.3524 nm. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: nA/(NA​a3).

quiz.q: How many atoms belong to one FCC unit cell?
quiz.explain: 8⋅81​+6⋅21​.

quiz.explain: The centre atom touches the 8 corners.

09.03.title: Defects and dislocations
09.03.html:
In the 1920s physicists calculated how strong a perfect metal crystal should be in shear. The answer was thousands of times stronger than any real metal. Either the theory was wrong, or real crystals had a defect that let them slip easily. In 1934 Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi independently proposed it: the dislocation. Seen directly in electron microscopes in the 1950s, dislocations explain why metals yield, why they work-harden, and why they can be bent instead of shattering.

The ideal shear strength

Slide one plane of atoms over another by x. The resisting stress must repeat every atomic spacing b. Frenkel modelled it as a sine:

τ(x)=τmax​sinb2πx​.

For small x this must reduce to Hooke’s law, τ=Gx/a with a the spacing between planes. Matching slopes gives

τmax​=2πaGb​≈2πG​.

For copper, G=48 GPa gives about 7.6 GPa. A pure copper single crystal actually starts slipping at around 0.5 MPa, some 15,000 times less.

Dislocations

Instead of a whole plane slipping at once, imagine an extra half-plane of atoms squeezed into the crystal: an edge dislocation. Under shear only the bonds near its core need to break and re-form, one row at a time, like moving a ruck along a carpet instead of dragging the whole carpet. The stress needed (the Peierls stress) is tiny for metals with wide, smeared-out dislocation cores. When it has crossed the crystal, the top has moved by one spacing b, the Burgers vector.

Most metallurgy is the art of making dislocations harder to move: grain boundaries, dissolved atoms, fine precipitates and tangles of other dislocations all get in their way (09.05).

A one-dimensional model

The Frenkel-Kontorova chain captures the idea. A row of atoms joined by springs k rests on a wavy substrate with wells one spacing apart. Push every atom with force F:

  • A perfect row slips only when F exceeds the substrate’s maximum restoring force.
  • Put one extra atom in (a kink, the 1D analogue of a dislocation). It glides at a far smaller push, because the atoms near it sit partway up the wells already.

Worked exampleIdeal strength and a gliding kink

  1. Copper: G/(2π)=7.64 GPa. Measured single-crystal yield is about 0.5 MPa, a ratio of 15,279.
  2. The chain: 60 sites, spring k=4, substrate amplitude V0​=0.2 (units where a=1). A perfect chain slips at F=V0​π=0.6283 per atom, verified: it holds at 95 % of that and slips at 105 %.
  3. With one extra atom, relaxed to a kink centred at site 29.5 (tightest spacing 0.715), bisection on F finds that the kink starts to glide at F=0.00766, 82 times less than rigid slip.
  4. Softer springs make a narrower kink that is harder to move: k=2 needs 0.06016 (10.4 times less than rigid slip) and k=1 needs 0.18940 (3.3 times less). Wide dislocation cores, as in FCC metals, are why those metals are so easy to deform.

Exercise 1Aluminium and iron

Estimate the ideal shear strength of aluminium (G=26 GPa) and iron (G=82 GPa). Annealed pure aluminium yields in tension at about 30 MPa, and soft iron at about 150 MPa. Taking the shear yield as half the tensile yield, how many times below ideal are they?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Aluminium: 26/2π=4.14 GPa. Shear yield about 15 MPa, so 4140/15=276 times below ideal.
  2. Iron: 82/2π=13.05 GPa. Shear yield about 75 MPa, so 174 times below.
  3. Both are polycrystals with some impurities, so they’re far stronger than a pure single crystal, but still two orders of magnitude below ideal. Only tiny defect-free whiskers and nanopillars come close to G/2π.

quiz.q: Ideal shear strength (GPa) of copper, G = 48 GPa. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: G/2π.

quiz.q: Ratio of ideal to actual shear strength for aluminium (G = 26 GPa, shear yield 15 MPa). Nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: 4.14 GPa / 15 MPa.

quiz.q: In the chain model, how many times less force did the kink need than rigid slip (k = 4)? Nearest whole number.
After an edge dislocation has crossed a crystal, the top half has shifted by…
quiz.explain: Slip of one lattice spacing.

quiz.q: Why are real metals so much weaker in shear than theory predicts?
quiz.explain: Moving a dislocation needs far less stress than rigid slip.
options: Dislocations let slip happen one row of bonds at a time

09.04.title: The tensile test
09.04.html:
Almost every strength number you’ll use, from yield strength in a datasheet to the allowable stress in a code, starts with one test: pull a standard bar until it breaks and record the load and the stretch. Reading that curve properly is a core skill.

Engineering and true stress

A round bar of original area A0​ and gauge length L0​ carries load P and stretches by ΔL.

  • Engineering stress and strain use the original dimensions: s=P/A0​ and e=ΔL/L0​.
  • True stress and strain use the current ones: σ=P/A and ε=ln(L/L0​).

Plastic deformation keeps the volume constant, AL=A0​L0​, so before necking

σ=s(1+e),ε=ln(1+e).

Reading the curve

  1. Young’s modulus E: the slope of the straight initial part. Fit a line well inside the elastic region, and use its zero crossing to correct for slack in the grips.
  2. 0.2 % offset yield Rp0.2​: most metals have no sharp yield point. Draw a line of slope E starting at 0.2 % strain; where it cuts the curve is the yield strength.
  3. Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the maximum engineering stress.
  4. Elongation: the strain at fracture (ductility).

Necking: the Considère criterion

The load is P=σA. As the bar stretches, σ rises (work hardening) but A falls. The load peaks when dP=0:

dεdσ​=σ.

Past that point any thinner spot carries more stress than its hardening can resist, and a neck forms. For a material with σ=Kεn (Hollomon), necking starts at a true strain of exactly ε=n, with

UTS=Knne−n.

So the hardening exponent n tells you how far a sheet can stretch evenly, which matters for forming car panels (09.22).

Worked exampleProcessing a raw test

A round aluminium-alloy bar, d0​=6 mm (A0​=28.274 mm²), extensometer gauge 30 mm. The data are synthetic so the answer is known: E=69 GPa, σ=380εp0.06​ MPa, with 5 N of load-cell noise and 0.5 µm of extensometer noise, 4000 points up to necking.

  1. Linear fit between 10 % and 40 % of the maximum load: E=68.69 GPa.
  2. 0.2 % offset line, with linear interpolation at the crossing: yield 259.90 MPa. The exact value is 380⋅0.0020.06=261.73 MPa, so the error is 0.7 %, inside the 1 % target.
  3. UTS 301.16 MPa against Considère’s Knne−n=302.28 MPa. Uniform elongation 6.55 % against 6.68 % predicted (the top of the curve is very flat, so noise blurs where the maximum is).
  4. At necking the true stress, 320.98 MPa, equals the hardening slope nKεn−1 = 320.98 MPa.

Exercise 1A steel test

A steel bar of 10 mm diameter yields (0.2 % offset) at a load of 27.5 kN and reaches a maximum of 36.1 kN at an extension of 9.0 mm over a 50 mm gauge. Find the yield strength, the UTS, and the true stress and true strain at the UTS.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A0​=π⋅102/4=78.54 mm². Yield =27500/78.54=350.1 MPa.
  2. UTS =36100/78.54=459.6 MPa.
  3. e=9/50=0.18. True stress =459.6⋅1.18=542.3 MPa; true strain =ln1.18=0.1655.
  4. By Considère that true strain is about the hardening exponent: n≈0.17, typical for mild steel.

quiz.q: UTS (MPa) of the steel bar (36.1 kN on 10 mm diameter). 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: Pmax​/A0​.

quiz.q: True strain at UTS for an engineering strain of 0.18. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: ln(1+e).

quiz.q: UTS (MPa) of a Hollomon material with K = 500 MPa, n = 0.2. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: Knne−n.

quiz.q: Necking begins when…
quiz.explain: Considère: dσ/dε=σ.
options: The true stress equals the slope of the true stress-strain curve

quiz.q: Why does the engineering stress fall after the UTS?
quiz.explain: True stress keeps rising.
options: The neck’s area shrinks faster than the material hardens

09.05.title: Hardening mechanisms
09.05.html:
Pure annealed iron yields at about 100 MPa. The steel in a Swiss watch spring yields at over 1500 MPa. It’s mostly the same iron atoms, with the same Young’s modulus. The difference is how hard it is for dislocations to move. Every strengthening method puts obstacles in their way.

Four ways to block dislocations

  1. Grain boundaries. A dislocation can’t easily cross from one crystal orientation to the next, so dislocations pile up at boundaries. Smaller grains mean shorter pile-ups and more boundaries. This gives the Hall-Petch relation
σy​=σ0​+d​k​,

with d the grain size, σ0​ the friction stress of the lattice, and k a material constant (about 0.74 MPa√m for mild steel, 0.07 for aluminium). It’s the only mechanism that raises strength without losing toughness.

  1. Solid solution. Dissolved atoms of a different size strain the lattice around them and pin dislocations. Brass (copper with zinc) and Al-Mg alloys use it. The effect grows roughly with the square root of concentration.

  2. Precipitation. Fine particles of a second phase. A dislocation either cuts through them or bows out between them and leaves a loop behind (Orowan). Bowing between particles spaced L apart needs a shear stress of

τ≈LGb​,

so closer particles mean higher strength. Age-hardened aluminium bike frames (6061-T6, 7075-T6) get most of their strength this way.

  1. Work hardening. Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and block each other. Cold-rolled sheet and drawn wire are strengthened this way; annealing undoes it.

To convert a shear stress on the slip plane to a tensile yield stress for a polycrystal, multiply by the Taylor factor, about 3.06 for FCC metals.

Worked exampleFitting Hall-Petch data

Synthetic data for a mild steel with σ0​=70 MPa and k=0.74 MPa√m, at eight grain sizes from 5 to 200 µm, with 4 MPa of scatter.

  1. Measured yields: 400.9 MPa at 5 µm, down to 127.7 MPa at 200 µm.
  2. Least squares on σy​ against d−1/2: σ0​=70.08±2.32 MPa and k=0.7376±0.0091 MPa√m. The fitted slope recovers 0.74 within 0.3 %, well inside its standard error.
  3. Predictions: 174 MPa at 50 µm, 303 MPa at 10 µm, 808 MPa at 1 µm. Ultra-fine-grained steels are made by controlled rolling.
  4. Orowan in aluminium (G=26 GPa, b=0.286 nm, Taylor factor 3.06): precipitates 1000 nm apart add 23 MPa; 100 nm apart, 228 MPa; 30 nm apart, 758 MPa.

Exercise 1Grain refinement

An aluminium alloy has σ0​=25 MPa and k=0.068 MPa√m. By how much does refining the grains from 100 µm to 10 µm raise the yield strength?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At 100 µm: 25+0.068/10−4​=25+6.8=31.8 MPa.
  2. At 10 µm: 25+0.068/10−5​=25+21.5=46.5 MPa.
  3. The increase is 14.7 MPa, much less than in steel, because aluminium’s k is ten times smaller. Aluminium alloys rely mainly on precipitation instead.

quiz.q: Yield strength (MPa) of the steel (σ₀ = 70 MPa, k = 0.74 MPa√m) at d = 20 µm. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: σ0​+k/d​.

quiz.q: Orowan shear stress (MPa) for G = 26 GPa, b = 0.286 nm, L = 50 nm. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Gb/L.

quiz.q: Yield increase (MPa) of the aluminium alloy refined from 100 µm to 10 µm. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: k(d2−1/2​−d1−1/2​).

quiz.q: Which mechanism raises both strength and toughness?
quiz.explain: Smaller grains also stop cracks.

quiz.q: Annealing a cold-worked copper wire…
quiz.explain: Recovery and recrystallisation remove the tangles.
options: Lowers its strength by removing dislocations
Changes its Young’s modulus a lot

09.06.title: Phase diagrams
09.06.html:
Melt copper and nickel together and let the mixture cool. Unlike a pure metal, it doesn’t freeze at one temperature. Over a range of about 25 °C, solid crystals richer in nickel grow inside a liquid richer in copper. Phase diagrams are the maps that tell you, for any composition and temperature, which phases are present, what they’re made of and how much of each there is.

Reading a binary diagram

The horizontal axis is composition (here, % nickel), the vertical one temperature. Copper and nickel dissolve in each other completely in both liquid and solid, so their diagram is a simple lens between two curves:

  • above the liquidus, all liquid;
  • below the solidus, all solid;
  • between them, liquid and solid coexist.

Inside the two-phase region, draw a horizontal tie line through your point. Its ends, on the liquidus and solidus, give the compositions xL​ and xS​ of the liquid and the solid.

The lever rule

How much of each phase? Conservation of nickel: if a fraction fL​ is liquid and fS​=1−fL​ is solid, then fL​xL​+fS​xS​=x0​. Solving,

fL​=xS​−xL​xS​−x0​​,fS​=xS​−xL​x0​−xL​​.

It’s like a lever balanced at x0​: each phase’s fraction is the length of the arm on the opposite side, divided by the whole tie line.

Where the curves come from

For an ideal solution, each component’s equilibrium between liquid and solid depends only on its own melting point Tm​ and heat of fusion ΔH:

xS​xL​​=exp[RΔH​(Tm​1​−T1​)].

Writing that for both copper and nickel gives two equations for xL​ and xS​ at each temperature, so the whole lens follows from four handbook numbers. Real alloys deviate somewhat, and many systems have eutectics, intermediate compounds and solid-state changes (09.07), but the tie-line and lever-rule reasoning is the same everywhere.

Worked exampleA 40 % nickel alloy

Copper: Tm​=1358 K, ΔH=13.05 kJ/mol. Nickel: 1728 K, 17.48 kJ/mol.

  1. Phase boundaries from the ideal-solution model (% Ni in liquid / solid): 1100 °C, 3.3 / 4.5; 1200 °C, 26.9 / 33.3; 1300 °C, 53.5 / 60.3; 1400 °C, 82.8 / 86.2.
  2. At 1235 °C: liquid with 35.9 % Ni and solid with 42.9 % Ni. Lever rule: 41.2 % liquid and 58.8 % solid. The two fractions sum to 1 exactly, and they reproduce the overall 40 % Ni to 10−12.
  3. Bisection on each boundary: the alloy starts to freeze at 1250.6 °C and is fully solid at 1224.5 °C.
  4. Cooled fast, the first solid (richer in Ni) has no time to even out, giving composition gradients called coring. A homogenising anneal fixes it.

Exercise 1Reading a tie line

On a measured Cu-Ni diagram at 1250 °C, the liquidus is at 32 wt% Ni and the solidus at 43 wt% Ni. An alloy has 35 wt% Ni. What fractions (by mass) are liquid and solid?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. fL​=(43−35)/(43−32)=8/11=0.727.
  2. fS​=(35−32)/11=0.273.
  3. Check: 0.727⋅32+0.273⋅43=35.0 wt% Ni.

quiz.q: Liquid fraction of the 35 wt% Ni alloy at 1250 °C (tie line 32 to 43 wt%). 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: (xS​−x0​)/(xS​−xL​).

quiz.q: Solid fraction for x₀ = 60 %, x_L = 53.5 %, x_S = 60.3 %. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: (x0​−xL​)/(xS​−xL​).

quiz.q: In a two-phase region, f_L + f_S equals…
quiz.explain: The lever rule’s built-in check.

quiz.q: The ends of a tie line give…
quiz.explain: Fractions come from the lever arms.
options: The compositions of the two phases

quiz.q: A Cu-Ni alloy cooled quickly through the two-phase region shows…
quiz.explain: Diffusion in the solid is too slow to keep up.
